en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 73.
The Training Rule on Deception.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks, having engaged in improper conduct, said as the Pātimokkha was being recited: "Let them think we have committed an offense through ignorance:
'Only now do we know this; indeed, this rule has come down in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta, and comes up for recitation every half-month.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How indeed can the group-of-six monks, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, say this:
‘Only now do we know that this rule, it seems, has come down in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta, and comes up for recitation every half-month’?
… [as before] … “Is it true, monks, that you say this while the Pātimokkha is being recited?”
“Only now do we know that this Dhamma, it seems, has come down in the Suttas, is included in the Suttas, and comes up for recitation every half-month.
“It is true, Blessed One,” [they replied].
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you say this while the Pātimokkha is being recited:
'Only now do we know that this rule, it seems, has come down in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta, and comes up for recitation every half-month'?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on]."
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever monk, while the Pātimokkha is being recited every half-month, should say:
‘Only now do I know that this rule, it seems, has come down in the Sutta, is included in the Sutta, and comes up for recitation every half-month.’”
If other monks should know that this monk has previously sat through two or three recitations of the Pātimokkha,
let alone more than that, there is no exemption for that monk on account of ignorance;
he must be dealt with according to the rule for whatever offense he has committed, and further delusion must be imposed upon him.
‘It is a loss for you, friend, it is ill-gotten for you, that when the Pātimokkha is being recited, you do not apply your mind with thorough attention.
This is the *pācittiya* offense regarding that delusion. “But whoever...
[refers to:]
Whoever is such a person … [as previously described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"Every half-month" means on the Uposatha day.
"While the Pātimokkha is being recited."
While they are reciting [the Pātimokkha],
one should speak thus after having committed an improper act.
If, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, one says:

“Let them know that I have fallen [into an offense] through ignorance,” thinking, “Only now do I know that this rule, which has come down in the Sutta and is included in the Sutta, comes up for recitation every half-month,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If other monks should know that this monk, who intended to deceive, has previously sat [at the recitation] two or three times;
When the Pātimokkha is being recited, what need is there to mention more? There is no exemption for that bhikkhu on account of ignorance;
whatever offense he has committed therein, he must be dealt with according to the Dhamma, and furthermore, delusion must be imposed upon him.
"And thus, bhikkhus, it should be imposed."
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
This monk named so-and-so, while the Pātimokkha is being recited, does not apply his mind with thorough attention.”
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha impose delusion upon the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
This monk, named so-and-so, did not apply his mind with thorough attention while the Pātimokkha was being recited.
The Saṅgha imposes a formal charge of delusion upon this monk, named so-and-so.
Whichever venerable one approves of the imposition of the charge of delusion upon this monk, named so-and-so, let him be silent.
"Whoever does not approve may speak.
The Sangha has charged the monk named so-and-so with delusion.
It is approved by the Sangha; therefore, by silence, I hold it to be so."
If one deceives someone who has not been charged with an offense of delusion, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one deceives someone who has been charged with an offense of delusion, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If it is a legitimate legal act and one perceives it as a legitimate legal act, yet one deceives [the person], there is an offense entailing expiation.
If one causes confusion while the legal action is legitimate, yet one is uncertain, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one causes confusion while the legal action is legitimate, perceiving it as illegitimate, there is an offense of expiation.
If one causes confusion while the legal action is illegitimate, perceiving it as legitimate, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
It has not been heard in detail;
it has been heard in detail fewer than two or three times;
nor was it for one desiring to delude.
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of the first offender.
The third training rule on causing confusion is concluded.
